data.name: Samsuddin
data.gender_notes: Samsuddin is used as a male name in Hindu naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: Samsuddin is a combination of two words: 'Sam' meaning protector and 'Suddin' meaning pure. It is believed that a person named Samsuddin is a protector of the universe and is pure at heart. The name Samsuddin carries the meaning “Protector of the Universe” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Hindu tradition and is also used in Hindi, Urdu, Bengali. Parents who choose Samsuddin usually hope their child will grow to embody protector of the universe and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: Samsuddin is a name that signifies divine protection and purity.
data.etymology: Samsuddin belongs to the Hindu linguistic tradition and is used in Hindu naming. Its recorded meaning is “Protector of the Universe.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Samsuddin total 5, giving a life-path number of 5. Number 5 is linked with Mercury and with the qualities of freedom, adaptability and curiosity.

data.cultural_impact: The name Samsuddin holds deep cultural significance in the Hindu community, as it is derived from Sanskrit language. The first part of the name, 'Sam,' is a term of respect and admiration often given to protectors and leaders in Hindu society. The second part, 'Suddin,' implies purity and divinity, which is a desirable characteristic in Hindu culture. This name may signify someone who embodies the qualities of a protector and maintains a high level of moral purity in their daily life.
data.spiritual_significance: From a spiritual perspective, the name Samsuddin implies a deep connection to the divine universe and a protector of its harmony. It suggests a person who has achieved inner purity and is devoted to serving and protecting the greater good. The name may represent someone who is responsible for preserving the balance and order in the world. Additionally, it is believed that a person named Samsuddin may have the ability to purify and protect the souls of those around them through their actions and words. The name instills a sense of reverence and respect towards the divine and the preservation of balance and order in the universe.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Samsuddin: Pure in Heart and Soul (Samm = pure, Suddin = heart/soul) In Hinduism, Samsuddin represents an individual who is deeply committed to spiritual growth and inner purity, striving to maintain a clear conscience and a heart free of worldly desires and attachments.

historical_references.reference: Samsuddin Ibrahim (1351-1358 AD) was the Sultan of Bengal who ruled over the territory that is now Bangladesh and West Bengal. He was a Turkish general who seized the throne after the death of his master, Sultan Ghiyasuddin Tughluq of Delhi.
historical_references.context: Samsuddin Ibrahim was a Turkish general who rose to power in Bengal after the death of his master, Sultan Ghiyasuddin Tughluq of Delhi.

historical_references.reference: Samsuddin Shahi (874-913 AD) was a Rashtrakuta king who ruled over the Deccan plateau in present day India. He was known for his religious patronage, constructing temples and funding Hindu scholars.
historical_references.context: Samsuddin Shahi was a Rashtrakuta king who was known for his religious patronage towards Hinduism.

modern_usage.modern_context: The name 'Samsuddin' has gained modern context in various fields, reflecting its rich history and diverse cultural significance. In academic research, historians have explored the role of Samsuddin Ilyas Shah, a 14th-century Bengali Sultan, in the development of Bengali Muslim identity and Islamic influences in the region. In historical fiction novels, authors such as Nadeem Mahomed and Anjali Joseph have featured Samsuddin as a character, providing insight into the complexities of the Bengali Muslim community and its historical experiences. Lastly, on social media platforms, the name is used as a badge of identity and pride within the South Asian diaspora, with many sharing stories of their ancestors who bore the name or highlighting its significance in Islamic and Bengali history.
